questions.text: Which part of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 contains the mandatory management-system requirements, such as leadership, risk assessment, internal audit and management review?

options.A: Annex A
options.B: Clauses 1 to 3
options.C: Clauses 4 to 10
options.D: ISO/IEC 27002

questions.explanation: Clauses 4–10 (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement) are the requirements for the ISMS. Annex A is tempting, but it is the reference list of controls that the risk treatment process uses; clauses 1–3 are scope, references and terms, and ISO/IEC 27002 is guidance.

questions.text: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 groups its Annex A controls into four themes. Which list is correct?

options.A: Organizational, people, physical, technological
options.B: Identify, protect, detect, respond
options.C: Preventive, detective, corrective, compensating
options.D: Policy, access, operations, compliance

questions.explanation: The 2022 edition has 93 controls in four themes: organizational (37), people (8), physical (14) and technological (34). "Identify, protect, detect, respond" are NIST CSF functions, and preventive / detective / corrective are control types, not themes.

questions.text: Under ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A, which theme contains the control on screening (background checks) of job candidates?

options.A: Organizational
options.B: People
options.C: Physical
options.D: Technological

questions.explanation: Screening is control 6.1, the first of the eight people controls, which cover the employment life cycle. Organizational is tempting because HR policies feel organisation-wide, but the 2022 edition puts screening under people.

questions.text: An ISMS risk assessment finds a risk above the organisation's acceptance criteria. Which is NOT an acceptable way to handle it?

options.A: Add controls to reduce the risk
options.B: Ignore it and record no decision
options.C: Stop the activity causing the risk
options.D: Share the risk, e.g. by insurance

questions.explanation: Reducing, sharing, avoiding and (formally) retaining a risk are all valid treatments, but each must be a documented decision that the risk owner approves. Retaining a risk is allowed; silently ignoring it isn't.

questions.text: A company certified to ISO/IEC 27001 hasn't held a management review of its ISMS for two years, although the security team meets every week. What should the auditor conclude?

options.A: An opportunity for improvement, not a nonconformity
options.B: No issue, since management review is optional guidance in the standard
options.C: A nonconformity: top management must review the ISMS at planned intervals
options.D: No issue, since the weekly security team meetings replace the formal review

questions.explanation: Clause 9.3 requires top management to review the ISMS at planned intervals, with set inputs and outputs. Team meetings are tempting as a substitute, but they aren't top management reviewing the whole ISMS, and a required activity that is missing is a nonconformity, not just an improvement point.

questions.text: Which function was added to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework in version 2.0 (2024)?

options.A: Prepare
options.B: Monitor
options.C: Govern
options.D: Comply

questions.explanation: CSF 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Govern is new and sits at the centre. "Monitor" and "Prepare" are common security words but are not CSF functions.

questions.text: A company sets up alerts in its SIEM for unusual logins outside working hours. Which NIST CSF 2.0 function does this mainly support?

options.A: Protect
options.B: Govern
options.C: Respond
options.D: Detect

questions.explanation: Detect covers finding and analysing possible attacks and anomalies, including continuous monitoring. Protect is tempting, but an alert doesn't stop the login; it reveals it.

questions.text: The board approves a cybersecurity risk strategy, sets roles and responsibilities, and defines security expectations for suppliers. Which NIST CSF 2.0 function covers these activities?

options.A: Protect
options.B: Govern
options.C: Recover
options.D: Identify

questions.explanation: Govern covers strategy, roles, policy, oversight and cybersecurity supply chain risk management. Identify is tempting (in version 1.1 some of this sat there), but in 2.0 it covers understanding assets and risks, not setting strategy.

questions.text: Several staff receive an email that appears to come from the CEO, urgently asking them to buy gift cards and send the codes. What kind of attack is this?

options.A: Denial of service
options.B: Brute-force password guessing attack
options.C: SQL injection
options.D: Phishing (social engineering)

questions.explanation: It tricks people, not systems, by impersonating a trusted sender and creating urgency. Nothing is flooded (denial of service) or guessed (brute force).

questions.text: Which of these is true multi-factor authentication?

options.A: Two different passwords entered one after the other
options.B: A password plus the answer to a secret security question
options.C: A password plus a code from an app on the user's phone
options.D: A username plus a long and complex password

questions.explanation: MFA needs factors of different types: something you know, have or are. The phone app is something you have. A security question is tempting, but it is a second thing you know, so it's the same factor twice.

questions.text: After a ransomware attack, a company finds that its backups, kept on a network drive in the same domain, were also encrypted. Which control would best have protected the backups?

options.A: A longer and more complex password for the backup service account
options.B: Stronger antivirus software installed on all employee laptops
options.C: Running backups more often to the same network drive as before
options.D: Offline or immutable backup copies kept apart from the main network

questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts everything it can reach, so at least one copy must be unreachable or unchangeable. More frequent backups to the same drive are tempting, but they would have been encrypted as well.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of full-disk encryption on a company laptop?

options.A: Stopping users from copying company files to USB drives
options.B: Protecting the laptop from being infected by malware
options.C: Keeping data unreadable if the laptop is lost or stolen
options.D: Protecting data while it is sent over the internet

questions.explanation: Disk encryption protects data at rest: without the key, a thief can't read the drive. Data sent over the internet is data in transit, which TLS protects, not disk encryption.

questions.text: Why should an application store user passwords as salted hashes rather than in encrypted form?

options.A: ISO/IEC 27001 requires hashing and forbids encrypting passwords
options.B: Salted hashes let administrators recover passwords users forget
options.C: Hashing makes the password database smaller and faster to search
options.D: A hash is one-way, so stored passwords can't simply be decrypted

questions.explanation: Encrypted passwords can be decrypted by anyone who gets the key; a hash can only be checked, not reversed, and the salt stops precomputed-table attacks. Recovering forgotten passwords is exactly what a hash prevents; users reset them instead.

questions.text: A vendor releases a critical patch for a vulnerability that is being actively exploited. Company policy applies all patches in a quarterly cycle. What should the auditor recommend?

options.A: Patch by risk, fixing critical exploited flaws within days
options.B: Keep the quarterly cycle so that all patches are treated alike
options.C: Wait for the next major version upgrade rather than patching
options.D: Apply every patch to production the same day, skipping tests

questions.explanation: A risk-based policy speeds up critical, actively exploited fixes while routine patches follow the normal cycle, still with suitable testing. Patching everything with no testing is tempting as the fast answer, but it trades one risk for another.

questions.text: Which is the most effective control against SQL injection in a web application?

options.A: Requiring HTTPS for every page of the website
options.B: Parameterised queries (prepared statements)
options.C: Encrypting the database files stored on disk
options.D: Hiding detailed error messages from all users

questions.explanation: Parameterised queries keep user input as data, so it can never be run as SQL. Hiding error messages is tempting and helps a little, but the injection still works; it just gives the attacker less feedback.

questions.text: Logged in as customer 1001, a tester changes the URL from /invoice?id=1001 to /invoice?id=1002 and sees another customer's invoice. What kind of weakness is this?

options.A: Broken access control
options.B: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
options.C: Weak encryption in transit
options.D: Denial of service

questions.explanation: The server doesn't check that the logged-in user may see the requested record (an insecure direct object reference), which OWASP groups under broken access control. XSS would inject a script into a page; nothing is injected here.

questions.text: The security team confirms that malware on one server is spreading to other machines on the network. What should they do first?

options.A: Email every customer to tell them about the attack
options.B: Wipe the server and rebuild it from scratch right away
options.C: Write the lessons-learned report for management
options.D: Contain it, e.g. isolate the server from the network

questions.explanation: While the malware is spreading, stopping it comes first; containment limits the damage and keeps evidence. Rebuilding is tempting but comes after containment and analysis, and wiping first destroys evidence.

questions.text: During a suspected breach, an IT administrator wants to shut down and reimage a compromised server at once to "clean it up". What is the main concern?

options.A: Reimaging a server usually takes longer than restoring a backup
options.B: Evidence such as memory and logs could be lost before analysis
options.C: All users of the server would need to reset their passwords
options.D: The operating system licence may become invalid after reimaging

questions.explanation: Shutting down erases memory, and reimaging overwrites the disk, so the team may never learn how the attacker got in or what was taken. Password resets may be needed anyway, but they are a separate step, not a reason to wait.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a post-incident (lessons-learned) review?

options.A: Improve controls so similar incidents are less likely
options.B: Decide which employee should be disciplined for the incident
options.C: Work out the insurance claim for the incident
options.D: Close the incident ticket as quickly as possible

questions.explanation: The review looks at what happened and how the response went, then feeds improvements back into controls and plans. It is deliberately not about blame, so people report honestly.

questions.text: What is the main difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?

options.A: A pen test tries to exploit weaknesses; a scan only finds them
options.B: They are the same test, sold under different names
options.C: A pen test covers the physical security of the building
options.D: A scan is done by hand, while a pen test is fully automated

questions.explanation: A scan is a mostly automated check for known weaknesses; a penetration test goes further and tries to exploit them, showing the real impact. "Scan by hand, pen test automated" has it backwards: scans are the automated part.
